transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Maya from Redwood. We have Ravi from SE and Lina on, thanks for making time.
[00:05] Alex Rivera: Hey all, Alex here, CTO at Polaris. We have Priya, Evan, and Sofia on the call.
[00:12] Maya Chen: Great, goal for today is a deep dive into GPU runtime profiling — kernel selection, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM comparisons, CUDA graphs behavior, and how that fits with your VPC/on-prem constraints. We'll keep it fairly technical. Feel free to interrupt.
[00:25] Priya Nair: Sounds good. We're especially interested in p95 latency under 200ms for chat completions at ~30 QPS and also how quantization will affect hallucination rates.
[00:35] Ravi Patel: Cool. To start, quick background on what Redwood's runtime does: we have a kernel selection layer that benchmarks short warmup runs and picks fast paths per layer and sequence length. We also support TensorRT-LLM kernels and a fallback path that looks a lot like vLLM's continuous batching on CUDA streams.
[00:50] Evan Cole: A question — how deterministic is kernel selection? We care about stable p95s across restarts and after autoscaling.
[00:58] Ravi Patel: Good question. Kernel selection is heuristic + profiling. On first load we do micro-benchmarks; we persist the selected profile so cold restarts use cached selection. The tricky part is CUDA graphs — they speed up steady-state but are sensitive to sequence length distribution changes. We handle that by regenerating graphs when distribution drifts exceed thresholds, but there's a warmup penalty.
[01:20] Alex Rivera: So if our prompt lengths vary a lot, we'd see recompile/regeneration pauses? How long are those pauses?
[01:27] Ravi Patel: Typically a graph regen is 100-300ms per affected batch-shape on modern A100/H100 nodes, but it depends on model size and TensorRT conversion time if we're using TensorRT-LLM. For large models + TRT conversion it could be multiple seconds on the first run, we try to do it async where possible.
[01:44] Priya Nair: For our workload we have a wide tail — 30% short prompts, 50% medium, 20% long — any recommended strategy?
[01:52] Ravi Patel: Two options: 1) use prefix-based caching/KV cache aggressively for the common prefixes to reduce actual decoding length, 2) shard by latency class — route short prompts to low-latency pools with different batching parameters/kernels and keep long prompts in a high-throughput pool. Smart routing reduces tail impact.
[02:10] Sofia Martinez: From security side, we need to ensure KV cache isn't persisted outside VPC and keys use our KMS. Does Redwood support customer-managed KMS and HSM-backed keys?
[02:20] Maya Chen: Yes — for Private deployments we support customer KMS integration and can prevent KV/disk persistence outside customer storage. We log accesses for audit. We'll share the KMS integration guide.
[02:30] Evan Cole: Back to kernel selection — we're comparing TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM paths. Can you provide practical differences for latency and memory usage?
[02:38] Ravi Patel: Short answer: TensorRT-LLM tends to give better throughput and lower per-token latency at large batch sizes and for models that map well to TRT kernels; vLLM-like paths (our native CUDA kernels with continuous batching) give better latency at small batch sizes and more predictable memory usage. TRT also uses additional memory for conversion and workspace; quantized TRT builds are tricky but can be very efficient.
[03:00] Alex Rivera: Any numbers? ballpark p95s for a 70B model on H100 at 16-token output: TRT vs vLLM?
[03:07] Ravi Patel: Ballpark on H100: TRT-LLM optimized -> p95 around 120-160ms at moderate batching (batch=8-16 effective), vLLM path -> p95 90-140ms at very small batch sizes but throughput is lower. There's overlap; TRT shines at parallelism/throughput. We'll share a spreadsheet with our benchmark runs — important caveat: these vary by model architecture and quantization.
[03:34] Priya Nair: About quantization — we need to go to 4-bit for cost, but worried about output quality. What do you recommend?
[03:41] Ravi Patel: We recommend mixed strategy: run evals on your prompt set. For many workloads 4-bit (QLoRA or GPTQ style) works with small quality delta; some instruction-following prompts degrade. Redwood Optimize can suggest per-model quant profiles and flag regressions via eval sets. We'll run an A/B during the POC.
[04:00] Evan Cole: CUDA graphs — you said they're sensitive. How do you manage dynamic sequence lengths in a production stream?
[04:07] Ravi Patel: We maintain a small set of precompiled graphs for common shapes and fallback to dynamic kernel execution for rare shapes. Also we use a late-binding strategy: decode with cached KV where possible so sequence length to decode is reduced. The runtime monitors miss rates and triggers offline/regeneration for new hot shapes.
[04:24] Alex Rivera: Any memory fragmentation or long-lived graph issues on long-running nodes?
[04:29] Ravi Patel: Fragmentation can happen when graphs allocate scratch memory and are not freed across many variations. We mitigate by pooling graph variants and resetting GPUs during rolling restarts. For Dedicated/Private we recommend a weekly drain/rolling restart window if you have highly variable shapes.
[04:45] Priya Nair: For our POC we'll do a 48hr run with realistic mix. What data do you need from us?
[04:50] Maya Chen: Priya — we'll need sample prompt sets, representative QPS patterns, and target SLOs. Also hints about on-prem NICs and whether you'll use RDMA.
[04:59] Priya Nair: We'll share sample prompts and traces by end of day tomorrow.
[05:03] Sofia Martinez: Security follow-up — SOC2, data residency, audit logs, and SSO. Also need to know how model artifacts are stored if we do Private.
[05:11] Maya Chen: We'll send SOC2 report and details on encryption at rest and KMS. For Private, model weights can be stored on customer-managed storage or encrypted volumes and we can integrate with your SSO for console access.
[05:20] Evan Cole: One more infra question — autoscaling impact on warm caches and KV coherence. If you scale down, do you lose hot cache and suffer cold p95 spikes?
[05:29] Ravi Patel: For Dedicated we offer a warm pool option where we keep a small baseline of GPUs hot to preserve KV cache and CUDA graph states; this reduces cost efficiency slightly but improves p95 stability. Cache warming on scale-up is typically 30-120s depending on model size and prefix reuse.
[05:45] Alex Rivera: About deployment mode — Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private — our security team leans to Private but costs matter. What are tradeoffs here re: perf?
[05:53] Ravi Patel: Private gives you most control: VPC-native networking, dedicated hosts, your KMS, and no egress. Performance can be slightly better due to network locality and pinned resources. Dedicated (Redwood-managed) gives similar perf but shared infra increases tail risk unless you buy reserved capacity. Hosted is fastest to onboard but less control. We'll model cost/latency tradeoffs for your specific QPS.
[06:13] Priya Nair: Any gotchas with TensorRT on Private infra? driver/CUDA compatibility?
[06:18] Ravi Patel: Yes — TRT versions are sensitive to CUDA/toolkit versions and driver stacks. On Private we recommend a validated AMI/container image that pins driver/CUDA/TRT combos; we'll provide a compatibility matrix. Without that, conversion failures or subtle perf regressions occur.
[06:33] Lina Gomez: Quick note — our runtime also supports per-tenant kernel profiles so you can pin kernel selection for a workload to avoid unexpected changes during rollouts.
[06:40] Priya Nair: Nice. Any perf regression monitoring?
[06:42] Ravi Patel: Redwood Console will surface per-route p50/p95, token-level latency breakdowns, and model-based regression alerts tied to your evals. We'll wire your prompt set into the eval pipeline.
[06:53] Alex Rivera: Let's talk concrete next steps then.
[06:56] Maya Chen: Recap: Redwood runs a 48hr benchmark on Polaris samples, share TRT-vLLM spreadsheet + CUDA graphs export, send KMS/SOC2/VPC docs, schedule POC scoping with Ravi and Priya next week.
[07:08] Priya Nair: Works for us. One ask — can you annotate the perf spreadsheet with which shapes triggered CUDA graph regen so we can correlate spikes?
[07:16] Ravi Patel: Yes, we'll include a column for graph-regens and timestamps.
[07:20] Evan Cole: Also include GPU GUC and driver versions used in runs.
[07:23] Ravi Patel: Will do.
[07:25] Sofia Martinez: And include audit log sample showing access patterns.
[07:28] Maya Chen: We'll redact PII but include sample audit events.
[07:31] Alex Rivera: Timeline — we'd like POC started next week and a decision in four weeks.
[07:36] Maya Chen: Sounds good. We'll target the benchmark start by 2026-12-07.
[07:40] Priya Nair: Thanks everyone.
[07:42] Maya Chen: Thanks all, I'll follow up with docs and the calendar invite.
[07:45] (call ends)

Notes: transcription shows occasional overlaps and replaced words (e.g., TRT sometimes transcribed as T-R-T or T R T), speaker labels sometimes generic in export then corrected. The transcript includes timestamps roughly every 15-60 seconds and occasional filler language.
